extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; poets, critics, and literary historians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for judging English poetry (lyrical, descriptive, didactic, and dramatic) with illustrations from poets such as Dryden, Thomson, Cowper, Butler, Bloomfield. Emphasises form, style, imagination, moral feeling, and suitability of tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of form (lyrical vs epic/dramatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyrical poetry ... deals in hieroglyphics and passing figures, which depend for effect, not on the working out, but on the selection. It is the dance and pantomime of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen form fits the subject and mode of delivery: lyrical pieces may be fit to be said or sung but 'not equally good to read'; they rely on selection of striking images rather than extended development. Example criticism: the Ode on St. Cecilia is excellent as 'poetical mechanism to be set to music, or recited,' but 'is not equally good to read.' Look for variety and rapidity of movement appropriate to lyric, and avoid forcing epic or dramatic expectations onto lyric material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loftiness and truth of character
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should have loftiness and truth of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical felicities and vivid images, evaluate whether work attains dignity and truthful portrayal of persons/subjects. Hazlitt notes Alexander's Feast 'wants loftiness and truth of character' despite lyrical strengths. Check for depth and authentic portrayal rather than mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs reliance on common-places
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the poetry of mere common places; do not take advantage of trite and mechanical common-places of imagery and diction as a relief to the Muse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify clichés, stock imagery, and rhetorical commonplaces used to pad or replace genuine inspiration. Hazlitt faults Dryden and Thomson when they 'eke out the lameness of the verse' or 'fill up the intervals of true inspiration with the most vapid and worthless materials.' Original, striking selection of images is prized over conventional phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to original force in adaptation and translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations from originals should preserve the impassioned declamation and force of the source; otherwise they 'break the force of the passion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating translations/adaptations (e.g., Chaucer/Boccaccio alterations), examine whether the adapter retains the emotional intensity and concentrated feeling of the original instead of weakening it to suit contemporary taste or decorum. Hazlitt cites Tancred and Sigismunda as an exception where force is retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantry, ostentation, and bombast
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems should not be pedantic or ostentatious in style, nor overload natural sentiment with 'a cloud of painted, pompous, cumbrous phrases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for gratuitous classical allusions, inflated diction, and bombastic patches that interrupt natural feeling. Hazlitt criticises passages which 'piece out a beautiful half line with a bombastic allusion' or 'overloads an exquisitely natural sentiment ... with painted, pompous ... phrases.' Style should serve feeling, not call attention to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of line-quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should not produce great lines only to be offset by bad ones: 'He seldom writes a good line, but he makes up for it by a bad one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate consistency across a poem or author's oeuvre: are excellent passages undermined by unevenness? Consistent craftsmanship (few blotting-worthy lines) is preferable to intermittent brilliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft, self-correction, and avoidance of chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not leave the business of writing to chance; exercise self-correction and labour—'He takes no pains, uses no self-correction; or if he seems to labour, it is worse than labour lost.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of revision and craft evident. Hazlitt praises work where feeling is spontaneous but faults authors who neglect revision and allow careless or slovenly workmanship. Good poetic art combines natural impulse with conscientious shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid multisensory description and total impression
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptive poetry should describe not to the eye alone, but to the other senses, and to the whole man; it should transfer the 'sum total of their effects, their varying influences on the mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge descriptive passages by their ability to evoke atmosphere (temperature, smell, sound, touch) and the 'vivid impression which the whole makes.' Hazlitt praises Thomson for conveying the glow of summer, the gloom of winter, and the feeling of the atmosphere—look for multisensory, immersive depiction rather than mere visual listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity and humanising the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'puts his heart into his subject, writes as he feels, and humanises whatever he touches.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sincerity and emotional truth: does the poet's feeling animate and humanise scenes/characters? Authentic emotion—whether tender, furious, or melancholy—should be perceivable and moving rather than merely ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral insight and reflective force
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral descriptions and reflections should be in an admirable spirit and written with force and fervour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When poetry includes moralizing or reflection, assess whether it contributes powerfully and truthfully rather than being didactic or flat. Hazlitt praises the Seasons' moral reflections as 'in an admirable spirit'—they should illuminate and enhance, not degrade the verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone and passion for subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone must fit the subject—e.g., a poem on liberty requires indignation against unjust power; 'Muse too easy and good-natured for the subject' is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the poet's temperament and chosen tone match the demands of the theme. A mismatch (gentle manner for a subject needing fury, or vice versa) weakens effect. Hazlitt notes Thomson's 'Muse was too easy and good-natured' for a powerful political subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic imagination and entering into others' passions
rubrics_metrics.description: To write tragedy or dramatic situations well, the author must 'put himself out of his way to enter into the situations and passions of others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characterisation and dramatic empathy: does the poet convincingly embody other minds and emotions? Hazlitt faults authors whose temperament prevents them from engaging with tragic passion or external situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, precision, and apt choice of topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of style, a certain precision and minuteness of graphical description, and a careful, leisurely choice of topics suited to one's genius are virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess economy and aptness of language, clarity of descriptive detail, and whether topics are well-matched to the poet's strengths. Hazlitt praises Cowper's precision and suitable topic choice even when noting other defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional resonance: moving the reader and infusing warmth
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital excellence: 'the power of moving and infusing the warmth of the author's mind into that of the reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems by their ability to move readers emotionally and transmit the author's sensibility. This intangible quality—'unbought grace'—is a key metric: does the poem convert private feeling into shared experience?

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and hearty sympathy versus finicalness/affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'finicalness of the private gentleman' and an affectation that 'repels common and hearty sympathy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for natural, unforced voice and generosity of feeling rather than self-conscious refinement or fastidiousness that distances readers. Hazlitt criticises Cowper's 'effeminacy' and excessive fastidiousness, which prevent broad sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, coherence, and avoidance of scattered cabinet-pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Works made of 'distinct studies, or highly finished cabinet-pieces, arranged without order or coherence' are less desirable than cohesive wholes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an author's pieces come together into a coherent whole with structural unity, rather than being merely a collection of polished but disconnected vignettes (as Hazlitt says of some of Cowper's works).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope, ambition, and the moral imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems should not be confined merely to the poet's immediate experience; they should clothe nature with the 'drapery of a moral imagination' and not be merely 'naked' depictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poet universalises experience and invests scenes with moral or imaginative depth. Hazlitt contrasts Bloomfield's faithful but narrowly experienced depiction with poets who elevate nature via moral imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register and appropriateness of description to subject (small vs sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the register of description to the subject: one may describe 'a piece of shell-work' well but fail to describe 'the New Jerusalem' (sublime/religious vision) in appropriate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging religious or sublime themes, ensure the poet attains sufficient elevation and fire; worldly or domestic diction may be apt for small subjects but inadequate for sublime matters (Hazlitt compares Cowper unfavourably to Bunyan for certain visions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of public taste and cultural context
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's success is affected by public taste and the state of manners, passions, and religious belief; 'public taste hangs like a millstone round the neck of all original genius that does not conform.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not strictly a stylistic quality, evaluate a poet's relation to contemporary taste: originality may be suppressed by cultural fashions; assess whether work is courageous and independent or panders to prevailing models. Hazlitt advises awareness of how education, manners, and public taste enable or constrain poetic achievement.
